title: Apple Metal — mount and forward
why: Run a Go layer on Apple GPU with an explicit lifetime.
what: Mount an identity Dense layer, inspect the Metal version and device, and forward a Float32 tensor.
body_extra:
Session ownership

Create a session with nativemetal.Mount, call Forward repeatedly and close it when finished. Mount accepts supported layers, Stack, Parallel and Grid layouts. The library is independent of welvet.cpp.

Requirements and backend boundaries

Go Welvet v1.3.0 uses the independent welvet.metal 0.68 library (mounted model ABI 1, segment extension 1). Install the library from its checkout:

cd ../welvet.metal
./scripts/macos_install_go.sh

Execution requires Apple silicon macOS and Go with cgo. Set WELVET_METAL_LIBRARY to override library discovery. Ordinary Go CPU use on Linux or Windows does not require Apple hardware. Unsupported hosts print SKIP in these examples; missing libraries on supported hosts report an error.

Go schedules work and manages memory; numerical Metal forward, backward and weight updates execute custom Apple GPU kernels. This is GPU acceleration through Metal, not Apple Neural Engine execution. Activations are Float32; FormatNone parameter storage supports 34 dtypes, with GDN restricted to Float32. Small examples demonstrate APIs; GPU launch costs can outweigh useful work at small shapes.

cpu-tiled means Go CPU; native_cpu means the separate welvet.cpp library; metal means the separate Apple GPU library. Neither native engine depends on the other. Examples 82–86 can use go run -tags welvet_metal . to exclude C++ linkage. Chapter 87 requires the normal cgo build for both native engines.

title: Apple Metal — Mamba parameter dtypes
why: Exercise native storage formats without changing the activation interface.
what: Run a seeded Mamba forward pass across all 34 native parameter dtypes, or select one with -dtype.
body_extra:
Storage versus arithmetic

-dtype all sweeps native parameter representations. It does not claim native Float64 GPU arithmetic or integer activation tensors: the Metal execution interface uses Float32 activations. Quantized FormatNone dtype storage and packed quantization formats are different coverage claims.

go run . -dtype all
go run . -dtype float16

Requirements and library installation: chapter 82.

title: Apple Metal — training modes
why: Keep repeated training updates in the mounted Metal session.
what: Train two Dense layers using one of the 29 numbered modes, with persistent Step Line state and real Grid layouts for Mesh modes.
body_extra:
Training families

-mode all exercises all 29 modes. Step modes retain their Line session across calls. Mesh modes use a three-cell Grid with disabled ingress and two active layers, advancing four ticks per call. These small demonstrations validate usage; they are not performance measurements.

go run . -mode NormalBP -steps 8
go run . -mode all -steps 8

Explicit mounted sessions keep updated weights native until SyncToGo(). Close discards any updates not returned to Go. See chapter 85 before saving.

Requirements and library installation: chapter 82.

title: Apple Metal — weight return and ENTITY save
why: Return trained weights to Go before executing or saving the Go model.
what: Train natively, explicitly SyncToGo, save an ENTITY, reload it and compare the native parameter snapshots.
body_extra:
Weight handoff

session, err := nativemetal.Mount(layer)
// Check err; defer session.Close().
// Repeat session.TrainMSE(...) as needed.
err = session.SyncToGo()
// Check err, then save through Go ENTITY IO.

Mount copies model state into a native session. The original Go parameters stay unchanged while that explicit session trains. SyncToGo() returns parameter bytes, scales and Float64 biases for Go saving. This saves model parameters, not a portable checkpoint of live Line, proxy, KV or rule state.

Use -out /path/model.entity to choose the output location. The default uses a temporary directory and prints it.

Requirements and library installation: chapter 82.

title: Apple Metal — JSON backend placement
why: Choose which layers run on Apple GPU while retaining ordinary Go training entry points.
what: Enable the Metal router and apply JSON placement to a Stack: layer 0 on Go CPU, layers 1–2 on Metal.
body_extra:
Explicit placement

The example embeds placement.json; use -config to load another file. nativemetal.EnableRouting() installs the router for its owner lifetime. placement.Stack applies immediate-child numeric layer keys. Grid placement also uses sector keys such as z,y,x,0 and local layer keys.

Routed execution maintains native sessions and returns updated parameters to Go automatically. Changing source weights remounts a session and resets transient native state. Automatic hardware/performance planning remains separate from explicit placement.

Requirements and library installation: chapter 82.

title: Apple Metal — mixed Go/C++/Metal
why: Split a single model between the independent native engines and Go.
what: Run a 13-layer Dense Stack: Go layers 0–3, C++ layers 4–8 and Metal layers 9–12; verify actual native calls during training.
body_extra:
Three engines in one Go model

Go CPU [0–3] → welvet.cpp [4–8] → welvet.metal [9–12] → Go result

The embedded placement.json uses go_cpu, native_cpu and metal. Install both native libraries and use the normal cgo build. The example reports successful C++ C ABI calls and Metal routing counters after five NormalBP updates.

Activations and parameters cross backend boundaries. Live backend-specific Line, proxy, KV or rule state is not migrated between engines. Backend support still depends on the selected layer configuration.

Requirements and library installation: chapter 82.

title: Apple Metal — Mamba results and stress runner
why: Measure real end-to-end Go bindings on sufficiently large models.
what: Display a labelled captured Mamba forward excerpt, then run the reproducible Go/C++/Metal stress matrix on your machine.
body_extra:
Captured forward excerpt

These user-supplied measurements were recorded on 2026-10-27. They are a historical snapshot, not a benchmark performed by loading this page. The five rows below are also printed by the example.

All 12 supplied forward rows reported Go/Metal exact-bit and tolerance agreement of 100%/100%. C++ unsigned storage differed in exact bits (uint64 21.2%, uint32 45.4%) while tolerance agreement remained 100%. This is numerical agreement, not prediction accuracy or a guarantee for future training runs.

Run the matrix

The bundled stress runner documentation describes all metrics and the full excerpt. It compares Mamba across 34 parameter dtypes and 29 training modes: 34 forward rows plus 986 training rows, or 1,020 rows, each covering three backends. Use the normal cgo build with both native libraries installed.

cd welvet/examples/apple_stress_test
./run.sh -profile smoke -samples 1 -iters 1 -steps 8
./run.sh

The default stress profile uses DModel 512, batch 8, sequence 32, three samples, three iterations, eight training steps and one warm-up. Reports include median wall time, setup and final weight-pull costs, speed ratios, time saved, exact-bit and tolerance agreement, and repeatability. CSV/JSONL/summary JSON are written progressively under results/.

Small-shape verification covered the full matrix; a separate stress-size Float32 NormalBP check measured Metal gains. That evidence does not claim the full large-shape matrix has already been timed. CPU/GPU numerical differences can grow over long training horizons. Best effort aims at exact agreement; project acceptance labels use 60/80/100 tolerance bands, not percentages of correct tensor elements or model accuracy.
